narrative:
The model estimated your chance of becoming a bad credit risk at 36%, and your application was denied because that estimate exceeded the lender’s approval cutoff. In practical terms, the model saw a meaningful risk of repayment difficulty, even though it was not predicting near-certain default.

The most influential factor was the short length of the credit you requested: 8 months, well below the approved-applicant average of about 19 months. That shorter exposure worked in your favor and pushed the decision toward good credit. The next most important factor was your checking-account status: being below 0 DM was an unfavorable signal and pushed toward bad credit. This mattered because most approved applicants had no overdrawn balance or a positive balance, while only about 12.6% were in the below-0 DM category. Your credit history rating of critical/other credits was the third most influential factor; in this case it leaned toward good credit rather than being the main driver of denial. Overall, the overdrawn checking-account signal was the clearest unfavorable factor among the top influences, and it was enough to keep the application below the approval standard.

To improve your chances, bring your checking account into a non-overdrawn position and keep it there for several months. Ask the lender what specific balance or documentation would strengthen a new application, and provide recent statements showing stable income and account management. You could also ask whether a guarantor or co-applicant would be considered.
